questions.statement: Which verb completes: "Look! I ______ the weekend on my history project"?
questions.context: At a school in San Jose, a student shows her desk mate a weekend project.

options.text: have spent
options.feedback: This works because the present perfect 'have spent' links the weekend to a visible result right now, as 'Look!' signals.

options.text: spend
options.feedback: 'Spend' is a present simple verb, and with 'I' it would need the third person 'spends' and would claim a habit.

options.text: am spending
options.feedback: The present continuous 'am spending' points to an action happening at this exact moment, but the weekend is already over.

options.text: spent
options.feedback: The past simple 'spent' reports only the finished time, so it loses the link with the result that 'Look!' is showing.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect connects a past action to a present result, often with 'look', 'already', 'just' or 'yet'. The past simple only reports the finished time.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb fits: "If she ______ in Puntarenas, she would join the club"?
questions.context: In Heredia, a student imagines studying in a different town next year.

options.text: lives
options.feedback: 'Lives' in an 'if' clause with 'would' describes a general habit, not the unreal situation a second conditional imagines.

options.text: is living
options.feedback: 'Is living' is the present continuous, and a second conditional 'if' clause never uses a continuous form.

options.text: lived
options.feedback: This fits because a second conditional joins a past simple 'if' clause with 'would' plus infinitive for an unreal situation.

options.text: will live
options.feedback: English never puts 'will' in the 'if' clause of a second conditional, because the modal belongs to the main clause.

questions.explanation:
The second conditional describes an unreal or imagined situation: 'if' plus past simple, then 'would' plus infinitive. Modals and continuous forms stay out of the 'if' clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version is passive: "The clinic will examine her tomorrow"?
questions.context: At a clinic in Alajuela, a nurse confirms tomorrow morning's appointment.

options.text: She will examine tomorrow.
options.feedback: This stays in the active voice and only changes the subject; in the passive the patient 'her' has to become the subject.

options.text: She will be examined tomorrow.
options.feedback: This works because the object 'her' becomes the subject and the verb turns into 'be' plus the past participle 'examined'.

options.text: She will have examined tomorrow.
options.feedback: 'Have examined' is the future perfect, which points to a result later, so it is wrong for a simple scheduled appointment.

options.text: She is being examined tomorrow.
options.feedback: 'Is being examined' is a present continuous passive, so it describes an examination in progress now rather than tomorrow.

questions.explanation:
In the passive the object becomes the subject, the verb becomes 'be' plus a past participle, and the tense is kept: 'will examine' becomes 'will be examined'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option builds a correct non-defining relative clause about the bus?
questions.context: A guide in La Fortuna tells her group which morning bus they will take.

options.text: The bus, that leaves at six, took my group to Arenal.
options.feedback: 'That' cannot introduce a non-defining clause, because commas mark extra information and only 'which', 'who' or 'what' can do that.

options.text: The bus which leaves at six, is the one my group took.
options.feedback: A comma cannot split a defining 'which' clause, since that clause identifies exactly which bus and cannot be removed.

options.text: The bus leaves at six, so my group took it to Arenal.
options.feedback: 'So' joins two independent clauses, so it produces two sentences instead of one clause carrying extra information.

options.text: The bus, which leaves at six, took my group to Arenal.
options.feedback: This works because the commas set off extra information and 'which' is followed by the full verb 'leaves'.

questions.explanation:
A non-defining clause adds extra information and is set off by commas. It uses 'which', 'who', 'whose' or 'what', never 'that', and it can be removed.

questions.statement: Which form fits: "He ______ milk the cows every morning at ten"?
questions.context: Don Ramon, a farmer in Guanacaste, remembers how he spent his childhood.

options.text: used to
options.feedback: This fits because 'used to' plus infinitive describes a habit or state that ended in the past, which suits his childhood.

options.text: has to
options.feedback: 'Has to' expresses an obligation that still exists now, so it cannot describe a habit that stopped years ago.

options.text: is used to
options.feedback: 'Is used to' means being familiar with an action and it must be followed by a gerund, such as 'is used to milking'.

options.text: was used to
options.feedback: 'Was used to' expresses past familiarity and it also needs a gerund, so it cannot be followed by the infinitive 'to milk'.

questions.explanation:
'Used to' plus infinitive marks a past habit or state that no longer holds. 'Be used to' needs a noun or gerund after it and means familiarity.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which form completes: "The guide suggested ______ a cup of the coffee"?
questions.context: On a coffee farm in Heredia, a guide recommends what the tour group should try.

options.text: to try
options.feedback: Verbs such as 'offer', 'decide' and 'promise' take 'to' plus infinitive, but 'suggest' normally takes the gerund 'trying'.

options.text: trying
options.feedback: This works because 'suggest' is one of the verbs that must be followed by a gerund, so 'suggested trying' is correct.

options.text: try
options.feedback: A bare infinitive after 'suggested' is not an accepted pattern; the verb needs either 'to try' or 'trying'.

options.text: to trying
options.feedback: 'To trying' glues an infinitive marker to a gerund, but only one of the two forms can follow the verb.

questions.explanation:
Verb patterns split into two groups: some take a gerund, such as 'enjoy', 'avoid' and 'suggest', while others take 'to' plus an infinitive, such as 'decide' or 'offer'.

questions.statement: Which modal fits: "Everyone ______ the questions, so Sofia scored 100"?
questions.context: In a classroom in Puntarenas, a teacher explains why one test was so easy.

options.text: can't have answered
options.feedback: 'Can't have' plus a participle firmly rejects a past possibility, so it would contradict the evidence of the perfect score.

options.text: mustn't have answered
options.feedback: 'Mustn't have' says the action was forbidden in the past, which is a statement about rules and not about deduction.

options.text: shouldn't have answered
options.feedback: 'Shouldn't have' criticizes a past choice that turned out badly, so it says nothing about how easy the questions were.

options.text: must have answered
options.feedback: This fits because 'must have' plus a participle draws a strong conclusion about the past from clear evidence.

questions.explanation:
Modals of deduction in the past use 'must have', 'might have' or 'can't have' plus a past participle. They express conclusions about evidence, not obligation or regret.

questions.statement: Which question is grammatically correct about the sources you gathered?
questions.context: At home in Tibas, a student plans the sources for a group presentation.

options.text: How much information have you gathered for the presentation?
options.feedback: This is right because 'information' is uncountable in English, so it takes 'much' in questions and never adds a final 's'.

options.text: How many information have you gathered for the presentation?
options.feedback: 'Many' is used only with countable plural nouns, and 'information' has no plural form in English.

options.text: How many informations have you gathered for the presentation?
options.feedback: Pluralizing the noun does not make it countable, so the uncountable noun still rejects the quantifier 'many'.

options.text: How much informations have you gathered for the presentation?
options.feedback: 'Informations' is not an English word, and 'much' would not fit a plural noun even if that form existed.

questions.explanation:
Countable nouns use 'many' in questions and 'a few' with 'count', while uncountable nouns such as 'information', 'advice' and 'homework' take 'much' and 'a little'.

questions.statement: Which version is passive: "The IT team must upgrade the computers in June"?
questions.context: A technician in Liberia explains next month's plan for the school computer lab.

options.text: All the computers in June must upgrade by the IT team.
options.feedback: The verb 'upgrade' is still active, so the objects remain agents of the action and nothing has been made passive.

options.text: All the computers must be upgrade in June by the IT team.
options.feedback: 'Must be' requires the past participle 'upgraded' to carry the passive meaning, since a bare infinitive cannot.

options.text: All the computers must be upgraded by the IT team in June.
options.feedback: This works because the modal 'must' is unchanged, the verb becomes 'be' plus 'upgraded', and the agent follows 'by'.

options.text: All the computers must be upgrading by the IT team in June.
options.feedback: 'Must be upgrading' builds a continuous passive, which suggests work in progress now instead of a scheduled future upgrade.

questions.explanation:
To form the passive, move the object to the subject, change the verb to 'be' plus a past participle and add 'by' plus the agent. Modals such as 'must' never change form.

questions.statement: Which option joins an unreal past action to a present result?
questions.context: A nurse in Quesada reviews a patient file before explaining the treatment.

options.text: If she takes the medicine now, she will be better tomorrow.
options.feedback: Both clauses are real here, so 'takes now' with 'will be better' is an ordinary first conditional prediction.

options.text: If she had taken it then, she would not be in the ward now.
options.feedback: This fits because 'had taken' marks the unreal past action and 'would not be' gives the present result.

options.text: If she took it then, she would not have been in the ward.
options.feedback: The 'if' clause is second conditional, so the result must be 'would not be', never the third conditional 'would not have been'.

options.text: If she will take it now, she would not be in the ward today.
options.feedback: A conditional 'if' clause never takes 'will', because English allows the modal only in the main clause of the conditional.

questions.explanation:
A mixed conditional uses 'if' plus 'had' plus a past participle for the unreal past action and 'would' plus infinitive for the present result, so past mistakes explain today's state.

questions.statement: Which sentence hedges a claim most appropriately in an academic essay?
questions.context: A student writes the conclusion of an essay about recycling in Escazu.

options.text: Recycling in Escazu is the best system in the whole world.
options.feedback: This claims an absolute 'best in the world' with no hedge, so it overstates the evidence an essay should present.

options.text: Recycling in Escazu works better than most other systems.
options.feedback: A plain comparative states the comparison as proven fact, and adding 'might' or 'may' is what keeps the tone academic.

options.text: Recycling in Escazu might be the most effective system.
options.feedback: This works because the modal 'might' softens a superlative claim, keeping the argument careful without losing the point.

options.text: Some people think that recycling in Escazu is effective.
options.feedback: Naming 'some people' shifts the claim to other speakers, so it reports an opinion instead of hedging the writer's own claim.

questions.explanation:
Hedges such as 'might', 'may', 'tend to' and 'appears to' soften a claim in academic writing, keeping a strong point while signaling that the evidence is not absolute.

questions.statement: Which question tag completes: "Nobody has ever hiked up to Poas"?
questions.context: A student in Alajuela checks a surprising statement during a group project.

options.text: has he
options.feedback: This is correct because the tag must agree with the negative subject 'nobody', so the tag becomes positive 'has he'.

options.text: hasn't he
options.feedback: 'Hasn't he' repeats the negative sense of 'nobody', so the tag would actually turn the statement into a contradiction.

options.text: don't they
options.feedback: 'Don't they' fails twice: it does not match the singular subject 'nobody' and it does not copy the auxiliary 'has'.

options.text: is he
options.feedback: 'Is he' cannot copy the present perfect auxiliary 'has', and it also ignores the negative subject 'nobody'.

questions.explanation:
Question tags copy the auxiliary of the statement and reverse its meaning. After 'nobody', 'never', 'no one' or 'hardly', the tag must turn positive.

questions.statement: Which comparison uses the comparative structure correctly?
questions.context: Two students in Heredia compare their scores on the university entrance exam.

options.text: Maria's score is more higher than Sofia's.
options.feedback: A short comparative ending in -er cannot also take 'more', so 'more higher' would double the comparative marker.

options.text: Maria scored as more points as Sofia did.
options.feedback: A comparative adjective cannot follow 'as', because the 'as ... as' frame already marks the two sides being compared.

options.text: Maria's score is as higher as Sofia's.
options.feedback: 'As' cannot be combined with the comparative suffix '-er', since the two markers would compete inside one expression.

options.text: Maria's score is twice as high as Sofia's.
options.feedback: This works because 'twice as ... as' is a valid ratio comparison, with the two 'as' parts on either side of the adjective.

questions.explanation:
Ratios use 'twice as' plus an adjective plus 'as'. The 'as ... as' frame marks equality, so a comparative ending like '-er' or 'more' cannot appear inside it.

questions.statement: Which article fits: "______ Arenal is a volcano in northern Costa Rica"?
questions.context: A writer in Monteverde introduces the volcano to visitors from the capital.

options.text: An
options.feedback: 'An' only marks a vowel sound before an unspecified noun, so it is the wrong choice between 'the' and no article here.

options.text: The
options.feedback: This is correct because English puts 'the' before single mountains, volcanoes and rivers, so the volcano is 'the Arenal'.

options.text: A
options.feedback: 'A' introduces one unspecified member of a class, which would wrongly suggest one volcano among many unnamed ones.

options.text: No article
options.feedback: Without any article the sentence reads as an item on a list, whereas a unique landform of this kind normally takes 'the'.

questions.explanation:
English uses 'the' before unique landforms such as single mountains, volcanoes and rivers. General or plural references take no article or 'a', but the name itself takes 'the'.

questions.statement: Which sentence is most appropriate in an email to a school coordinator?
questions.context: A student emails the coordinator of a class trip to San Isidro del Monte.

options.text: Hey, just wondering if maybe you could sort of let us go, thanks.
options.feedback: The fillers 'just', 'maybe' and 'sort of' with the contraction sound casual, so the request sounds unprepared in an official email.

options.text: Hey!! Can we PLEASE go?? It is going to be sooo fun!!!
options.feedback: The repeated capitals and question marks with 'sooo' belong to chat messages between friends, not to a request for permission.

options.text: I am writing to ask whether the group may visit next Friday.
options.feedback: This works because the polite full form 'I am writing to ask whether' suits a formal request addressed to a member of staff.

options.text: We would, hypothetically, perhaps consider the excursion soon.
options.feedback: Over-hedged wording such as 'would, hypothetically, perhaps consider' sounds evasive, so the sentence never makes a clear request.

questions.explanation:
Register must match the audience. An email to a coordinator uses full forms, polite structures such as 'I am writing to ask whether', and no slang or texting abbreviations.

questions.statement: "We will export less next year," said the farmer. Which report is correct?
questions.context: A journalist in Cartago interviews a coffee farmer about the April frost.

options.text: The farmer said we will export less the next year.
options.feedback: 'Will' cannot survive a past reporting verb unchanged, and 'the next year' here would still be measured from the moment of speaking.

options.text: The farmer said we exported less the next year.
options.feedback: 'Exported' is the past simple, so it asserts that the exports already fell, while the original spoke about a future drop.

options.text: The farmer said we would export less next year.
options.feedback: 'Next year' is a deictic time word, so leaving it unchanged makes the reported future point to the reader's own year.

options.text: The farmer said we would export less the following year.
options.feedback: This works because 'will' becomes 'would', the pronoun 'we' stays, and 'next year' becomes 'the following year'.

questions.explanation:
Reported speech shifts the modal 'will' to 'would' and moves time words one step away: 'next year' becomes 'the following year' and 'now' becomes 'then'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which linker fits: "The bus is cheap ______ it is slow at rush hour"?
questions.context: A writer links two ideas in an essay about public transport in San Jose.

options.text: so
options.feedback: 'So' expresses a result, so it would claim that low fares are caused by the slowness, which is not the intended meaning.

options.text: even though
options.feedback: This works because 'even though' marks a contrast against expectation, setting a benefit against an unexpected drawback.

options.text: because
options.feedback: 'Because' gives the reason for the first clause, so it would claim that the cheap fares exist because the buses are slow.

options.text: otherwise
options.feedback: 'Otherwise' points to a negative result if something fails to happen, so it cannot join two true statements about the system.

questions.explanation:
'Even though' introduces a contrast against expectation. 'So' shows result, 'because' shows cause and 'otherwise' shows a negative consequence, so each changes the logic.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which preposition fits: "She succeeded ______ passing all her subjects"?
questions.context: A student in Cartago describes how she organized her study week before the exams.

options.text: to
options.feedback: 'Succeed' never takes 'to' plus an infinitive, so this wrongly copies the pattern of 'manage to', which does need 'to'.

options.text: for
options.feedback: 'For' marks a reason or a substitute with other verbs, but 'succeed' accepts no preposition except 'in'.

options.text: in
options.feedback: This is correct because 'succeed in' is a fixed collocation that keeps its preposition even before a gerund.

options.text: at
options.feedback: 'At' belongs after nouns such as 'success' or 'skill', so attaching it to the verb 'succeed' breaks the pattern.

questions.explanation:
Prepositions belong to a verb's fixed pattern. 'Succeed in', 'depend on', 'insist on' and 'apologize for' keep their preposition even when a gerund follows.

questions.statement: Which revision is clearest for "The program that the town started cuts waste"?
questions.context: A student edits the conclusion of his essay about recycling in Guanacaste.

options.text: In my opinion, the town's recycling program has begun to cut waste.
options.feedback: This works because it drops the useless relative clause, so the claim is shorter and the main verb reaches the reader directly.

options.text: The recycling program has begun, and that is what I think about it.
options.feedback: Adding a coordinate clause with 'and that is what I think' lengthens the sentence again and replaces the point with a comment.

options.text: In my opinion I think that recycling has cut waste and it is a good thing.
options.feedback: The revision keeps the weak 'In my opinion I think that' pair and adds a second idea, so it loses the conciseness it wanted.

options.text: The program has been cutting waste since it started and is much better now.
options.feedback: 'Has been cutting since it started' with 'much better now' piles on extra claims, so the conclusion ends less focused.

questions.explanation:
Clear revision removes doubled framing such as 'In my opinion I think', cuts unnecessary relative clauses and keeps one idea per sentence, because wordiness hides the main claim.

questions.statement: Which reduction is correct: "Birds which were recorded in the forest fly at dusk"?
questions.context: A researcher in Upala describes the birds she recorded near a banana plantation.

options.text: Birds was recorded in the forest fly at dusk.
options.feedback: 'Was recorded' is singular and passive, so it disagrees with the plural subject 'Birds' inside a reduced relative clause.

options.text: Birds were hearing in the forest fly at dusk.
options.feedback: 'Were hearing' is a past continuous form, while a reduced relative clause uses only a bare past participle without an auxiliary.

options.text: Birds are recorded in the forest fly at dusk.
options.feedback: 'Are recorded' is present passive, so it changes when the recording happened and leaves the sentence without a full verb phrase.

options.text: Birds recorded in the forest fly at dusk.
options.feedback: This works because the passive relative is reduced to a past participle phrase and 'fly' still agrees with plural 'Birds'.

questions.explanation:
A reduced relative clause keeps only the past participle, but it must still agree with the subject in number and tense: 'birds which were recorded' becomes 'birds recorded'.
